analysis.one_liner: Gives drugmakers longer patents and tax credits to develop new antibiotics and antivirals.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to three House committees in March 2007 and never received a hearing or a vote before Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill responds to the growing problem of drug-resistant infections, citing roughly 2 million hospital infections and 90,000 deaths a year in the U.S., most resistant to at least one drug. To coax companies back into an antibiotic market they have been leaving, it extends patents on new infection-fighting drugs, tests, and vaccines, gives a 50% tax credit for related research, a 20% credit for building manufacturing plants, fast-tracks FDA review, and has the National Institutes of Health help small companies pay for late-stage trials. It also creates a commission to identify the most dangerous resistant pathogens and directs the FDA to write clinical trial guidelines for antibiotics.
analysis.who_benefits: Pharmaceutical and biotechnology companies gain the most directly: longer patent monopolies on new antibiotics, antivirals, diagnostics, and vaccines, a 50% tax credit on qualified research expenses, and a 20% credit for building manufacturing facilities. Small manufacturers additionally get federal grants for end-stage clinical trials. If the incentives work, patients facing drug-resistant infections would eventually gain access to new treatments.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Drugmakers and patients with resistant infections

how_it_helps.text: Extends the patent term for a 'qualified infectious disease product' by up to 2 years beyond the normal term, in addition to restoring time lost during regulatory review.
Creates a tax credit worth 50% of qualified infectious disease research expenses and a 20% investment credit for manufacturing facilities for these products.

Requires the Secretary of Health and Human Services to designate these products as fast-track for FDA approval, and directs NIH to expand grants helping small manufacturers run end-stage clinical trials.
Establishes a permanent Commission on Infectious Diseases Product Development to identify drug-resistant pathogens that threaten public health and recommend how to address them.
Targets a documented public health threat: the bill's findings cite about 2 million hospital-acquired infections and 90,000 deaths annually, with about 70% resistant to at least one drug.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers bear the cost of the research and manufacturing tax credits through foregone federal revenue. Consumers and health systems bear higher drug prices on the affected products, because the extra years of patent protection delay cheaper generic competition. If no new drugs result, the public bears the cost with nothing to show for it.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers and future users of these drugs

drawbacks.text: The main incentive is extra years of patent monopoly, which keeps prices higher and delays generic versions of exactly the drugs the bill targets — a cost borne by patients, hospitals, and insurers.

The research credit and the 20% manufacturing facility credit reduce federal revenue, effectively having taxpayers subsidize drug development that companies will then sell under extended monopoly protection.

The new commission is weighted toward industry: 12 of its 19 voting members are appointed from the infectious disease medical, research, pharmaceutical, and biological communities, and its first report is directed to examine the potential benefits of medical liability relief — giving industry a formal role in steering the program.

Incentives and fast-track designations do not guarantee that new antibiotics actually reach patients; the bill offers public money and monopoly time in exchange for a pipeline that may or may not materialize.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Drug-resistant bacteria are a genuine, growing threat, and major drugmakers were exiting the antibiotic market because these drugs are less profitable than long-term treatments — so some intervention was warranted. But the bill's chosen tool is to hand industry longer monopolies and large tax credits rather than to fund development directly, meaning much of the benefit flows to drugmakers and the public pays through higher drug prices and lost tax revenue, with no guarantee new antibiotics result. It is a real public-health bill wrapped around a substantial industry giveaway, and it never got far enough for anyone to weigh that tradeoff in the open.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in three House committees and their subcommittees for nearly two years without a hearing or vote, and it died when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Rep. Brian Baird introduced the bill on March 13, 2007, joined by Reps. Cubin and Matheson, and it was referred to the Energy and Commerce, Judiciary, and Ways and Means Committees.
Two weeks later it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health; a month after that, to the Judiciary Subcommittee on Courts, the Internet, and Intellectual Property.
No further action was ever taken: none of the three committees held a markup or scheduled the bill for a floor vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 2009.
The bill attracted minimal visible support — four cosponsors (3 Republicans, 1 Democrat) — and no recorded opposition, so it simply expired with the Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The status quo won: no new antibiotic incentives were enacted, so the Treasury kept the tax revenue and generic competition on existing drugs was not further delayed, but the promised new antibiotics for resistant infections never materialized and resistant bacteria continued spreading.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo — no incentives, no new antibiotics

for.name: Rep. Brian Baird
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to create patent, tax, and regulatory incentives for antibiotic and antiviral development.

for.name: Reps. Barbara Cubin and Jim Matheson
for.what_they_did: Joined Baird in introducing the bill on its introduction day.

for.name: 3 House Republicans and 1 House Democrat
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, bringing total cosponsorship to four.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on March 13, 2007, sent it to the Health Subcommittee two days later, and never held a markup or moved the bill.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (Courts, Internet, and Intellectual Property Subcommittee)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on March 13, 2007, sent it to the IP Subcommittee on April 20, 2007, and never acted further.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral for the bill's tax credit provisions on March 13, 2007, and never acted on them.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan — a Democratic sponsor with three Republican and one Democratic cosponsors — and no votes were ever taken, so no partisan split over the bill ever surfaced.

industries.note: The bill hands them up to 2 extra years of patent life plus restored review time on new infection products, plus a 50% research tax credit — a large giveaway designed to pull them back into antibiotics. New drugs would help patients, but the longer monopolies mean higher prices and delayed generics on those same drugs.

Small manufacturers would get NIH grants to pay for expensive end-stage clinical trials, plus the research and manufacturing tax credits. Their interest in a viable pipeline for resistant infections runs alongside the public's.

Extra patent years on qualified infectious disease products delay generic versions of those drugs. Cheaper generics serve the public's interest in affordable treatment, so this industry's interest here runs alongside patients'.

Diagnostic tests for resistant infections are included among qualified products eligible for fast-track review, patent extension, and the research credit. Rapid diagnostics would also help doctors prescribe correctly and slow resistance.
